title: Where forgiveness is
hook: Kabir, in the Guru Granth Sahib: where there is forgiveness, there is God (Guru Granth Sahib 1372)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kshama: forbearance, listed among the Gita's divine qualities beside vigor and fortitude. Your line was packed in with the steel.

A couplet built like a map. Where this is, there's that. Where this other thing is, there's that other thing. Pair after pair, plain as directions to a neighbor's house. It sits near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, on page thirteen seventy-two, in a run of short couplets, saloks, by Kabir, the weaver poet whose verses the Sikh Gurus gathered into their book. Then the last pair changes what kind of map it is.

In paraphrase, Kabir says: where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death. And where there is forgiveness, there is God himself. The first pairs read like cause and effect. Wisdom leads to right living. Lies lead to wrongdoing. Greed leads to ruin. Then the last pair breaks the pattern. Forgiveness doesn't lead to a reward, or a better mood, or a good reputation. It's the place where God is found. Two words carry it. The word for forgiveness in the Gurmukhi text is khima. And the word at the very end, for God, is aap: himself, God's own self. Not a gift sent from God to the forgiving person. God, present, where forgiveness is happening. The couplet is by Kabir, not one of the Sikh Gurus. Yet it sits in the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru, alongside the Gurus' own hymns. The Gurus included voices from beyond their own circle, Hindu and Muslim saints among them, where those voices said what the Gurus heard as true. So a weaver's line about forgiveness is sung and read in gurdwaras as scripture. Set it beside yesterday's. The Gita listed kshama as a quality of divine nature. Kabir puts it as a place: find forgiveness, and you've found where God is.
screen: `WHERE THIS IS, THERE IS THAT.` · `THE LAST PAIR BREAKS THE PATTERN.` · `KHIMA, AND AAP.` · `A WEAVER'S VOICE IN THE GURU.` · then, large: `WHERE FORGIVENESS IS, GOD HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Find one small thing to forgive from this week, a borrowed thing returned scratched, a remark at dinner, and bring it up clearly. Then set it down here, the way you'd set down a cup, without waiting to feel finished, and stay a few breaths with the space where it was. If you pray, you can say a line of Kabir's or your own tradition's words; if not, simply rest there.
Khima. Kabir's word for forgiveness in the Guru Granth Sahib, from the couplet where there is forgiveness, there is God himself. Today's word.
Your line: God's own self, present there. Not a reward for forgiving, but a presence in it. See you tomorrow.

notes: Kabir's salok paraphrased (modern translations are not public domain; Macauliffe 1909 may include it but the writer isn't certain of his wording). Gurmukhi as remembered: ਜਹਾ ਗਿਆਨੁ ਤਹ ਧਰਮੁ ਹੈ ਜਹਾ ਝੂਠੁ ਤਹ ਪਾਪੁ ॥ ਜਹਾ ਲੋਭੁ ਤਹ ਕਾਲੁ ਹੈ ਜਹਾ ਖਿਮਾ ਤਹ ਆਪਿ ॥ Confirm Ang 1372 and salok number 155.
'Kaal' rendered as death; some render it 'the messenger of death'. 'Aap' rendered 'God himself'. Confirm.
